newsitem.title: USA: Former G7 aides see no formal yen support-RFTV.
newsitem.headline: Former G7 aides see no formal yen support-RFTV.

text.p: Market forces will ultimately return the soaring dollar/yen exchange rate to a lower, more sustainable level, obviating the need for the world's major nations to take formal steps to weaken the dollar, former economic officials said.

As the Group of Seven industrialized nations meet in Berlin next weekend, they should focus on stabilizing currency markets, not directing them, according to three former G7 financial aides interviewed on Reuters Financial Television.
The officials did not rule out official intervention as a useful tool to smooth out currency market moves or minimize drastic fluctuations.
But the current environment, with the dollar having risen over 50 percent from its post-World War II low at 79.75 in April 1995, does not warrant intervention, they said.

"I wouldn't think that the exchange rates are that far out of line vis-a-vis the cyclical and fundamental tendencies of the various economies that we need some kind of strong statements about exchange rates at this stage," said John Crow, former Bank of Canada Governor.
While the G7 should always support strong currencies for each of its members, now is not the time to weigh in against the dollar, Crow added.

"I don't think anybody should ever be against statements supporting currencies. If by the same token, you're suggesting the U.S. dollar should be weaker, I think the Americans might have some problems with that kind of statement," Crow added.
